lesson.title: Packet Capture: The Machinery Behind Wireshark and Tcpdump
lesson.summary: Packet capture is the general technique of copying packets off a network interface as they pass by, the shared foundation that both Wireshark and tcpdump are built on top of.
lesson.body:
Wireshark and tcpdump feel like different tools, one graphical, one command-line, but they are really two front ends for the same underlying capability: packet capture. Understanding that capability on its own, separate from either tool, explains a lot about what capturing traffic can and cannot do, and where its limits come from.

At its core, packet capture works by asking a network interface to hand a copy of every packet it sees to a capturing process, rather than only the packets addressed to that machine. Normally, a network interface quietly discards frames not addressed to it. Capturing usually requires putting the interface into a mode where it accepts everything it physically receives, and then copying those frames up through the operating system to the capturing application, commonly through a library such as libpcap on Linux and macOS or npcap on Windows. Both Wireshark and tcpdump are, underneath, clients of this same capture layer, which is why a capture file saved by one opens cleanly in the other: they typically use the same pcap or pcapng file format.

One detail that matters in practice is filtering location. A filter can be applied at capture time, inside the kernel, before packets are even copied to the application, or afterward, as a display filter over an already-captured set. Capture-time filtering is far cheaper: on a busy interface pushing tens of thousands of packets per second, copying every single one up to user space and only discarding most of them afterward can cause the capture tool to fall behind and silently drop packets, leaving gaps in the record without any obvious warning. This is why both Wireshark and tcpdump support capture filters, not just display filters, and why capturing narrowly (a specific host, port, or protocol) is usually preferable to capturing everything and filtering later, especially on high-traffic links.

A second detail is where you capture matters as much as how. On a modern switched network, a host's own interface generally only sees traffic addressed to it, plus broadcast and multicast, not the traffic between two other machines on the same switch. If you need to observe traffic between an application server and a database server on separate ports of the same switch, capturing on your own laptop plugged into a third port will show you nothing useful. You need either a switch port configured to mirror traffic from the ports you care about, often called a SPAN port, or a physical network tap inserted in line, or you need to run the capture directly on the two endpoints themselves and compare timestamps afterward. This is a common mistake for people new to packet capture: assuming that plugging into the network anywhere lets you see any traffic you want, when in reality visibility depends entirely on where in the topology the capture point sits.
